turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I came in because... I guess my temper's been getting the better of me lately. 

The other day, I completely snapped on a board call. It was just over a small question about the facility budget—nothing that should have set me off—but I just lost it on 'em. And... well, that is just not how I run my company. It's definitely not how I treat people. So I figured I needed to come in and talk to somebody about it.

symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient describes losing their temper and having an angry outburst ('completely snapped' and 'lost it on 'em') over a minor question on a board call.

turns.doctor_question: Has this kind of irritability been a new thing over the past few weeks, or is it something that's been part of how you've felt for a much longer time?
turns.patient_response: No, it's definitely a new thing. It's really only been going on for about six days now. It started right after... well, there was an explosion and a fire during a walkthrough I was doing. So, yeah, just since then.

turns.doctor_question: Since the explosion, have you found yourself having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the event, or going out of your way to avoid anything that reminds you of it?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I have. Not really nightmares, but the memories... they definitely pop up when I don't want them to. 

I'll be right in the middle of a phone call, or just sitting at my desk looking at the numbers, and the blast—and that fire over by the loading area—it just jumps right back into my head. It's almost like a bad film I didn't ask to see. I'm not trying to think about it at all, it just forces its way in.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient explicitly confirms recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive memories of the explosion and fire forcing their way into their mind during daily activities.

turns.doctor_question: Since the explosion, have you noticed times when you feel oddly detached from yourself or your surroundings—like you're in a daze, watching things happen from outside your body, or like things around you don't feel quite real?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, I have noticed something like that. Sometimes when I'm taking calls from the house, I'll be talking and... well, the room just starts to look kind of distant. And my own voice sounds strange to me. 

It's hard to explain, but it's almost like I'm watching myself talk instead of being fully there in the room. It's a very odd feeling.

symptom_reasoning.S082: The patient confirms experiencing depersonalization and derealization, describing the room looking distant, their voice sounding strange, and feeling as though they are watching themselves talk.

turns.doctor_question: Since the explosion, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, conversations, or activities that remind you of what happened?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I have. I've been keeping away from the new building entirely. And it's not just the site itself... even the paperwork is getting to me. 

The mortgage folder, the safety reports—they're just sitting there unopened. I tell myself I need to look at them, but the minute I reach for them, my stomach just drops. So I just leave them be. I guess I'm avoiding anything that has to do with it.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly confirms avoiding reminders of the explosion, including staying away from the building site and leaving related paperwork unopened.

turns.doctor_question: Since the explosion, have you noticed any changes in your sleep, like trouble falling or staying asleep, or finding yourself more jumpy or easily startled than usual?
turns.patient_response:
My sleep hasn't really changed much, to be honest. But I am definitely a lot more jumpy. 

If a door shuts hard somewhere in the house, or... even if the printer just kicks on behind my desk, I jump like something went off again. It really gets to me. It takes me a good few minutes just to get my hands steady after it happens.

symptom_reasoning.S080: The patient explicitly confirms being much more jumpy, jumping at everyday sounds like doors shutting or printers starting, and taking minutes to calm down.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient explicitly states that their sleep has not really changed much.

turns.doctor_question: Since the explosion, have you had trouble remembering important parts of what happened during the incident itself?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't had any trouble with that. Honestly, I remember the whole thing pretty clearly. I know exactly where I was standing and what happened when it went off. I haven't forgotten any of it... my memory of that day is perfectly fine.

symptom_reasoning.S071: The patient explicitly denies having trouble remembering the event, stating they remember the entire explosion clearly and haven't forgotten any of it.

turns.doctor_question: Would you say these reactions—the flashbacks, jumpiness, and avoidance—have been getting in the way of your ability to do your job or handle your daily responsibilities?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I'd say it is. I mean, I'm still technically working, but... I'm definitely delaying decisions about the facility. I just find myself leaning on others for calls I would normally handle myself. We had a board call recently, and my reaction on that call... well, it made me realize that this is really starting to affect my judgment and my leadership. So, yes, it is getting in the way of my job.
